traveler: Élisabeth Sonrel (Élisa Marie Stéphanie Adrienne Sonrel)
title: The Doctor's Easel to the Cemetery of Sceaux: Tours, the Salons, and the Breton Coast
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Tours, birth in a physician's house
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In a physician's house at Tours, on the Loire, a daughter is born to Nicolas Stéphane Sonrel and given four names: Élisa Marie Stéphanie Adrienne. The father is a military doctor who paints on his leave, and he will be the first person to put a brush in her hand. Nothing else of the birth survives in the record, no street, no hour, no godparents. What survives is the date, and a father who draws for his own pleasure and goes on teaching her long after the first lesson.
suggested_refs: Civil birth register of Tours, 17 May 1874, for Élisa Marie Stéphanie Adrienne Sonrel

stops.name: Tours, the first lessons at her father's easel
stops.date_confidence: inferred; no source dates the childhood lessons, and the studio's address is nowhere recorded, so this pin is the Tours centroid rather than a located building
stops.campa: Before any academy takes her, the girl learns to draw beside a man who learned it as an amateur. The discipline is the old one, a hand copying a hand, and it runs for years in a room whose address nobody wrote down. Later accounts call this her true schooling, more decisive than the Parisian atelier that follows. Tours gives her the Loire light and a physician's patience with slow work. What Tours cannot give her is a jury. That is two hundred and thirty kilometres north, and she has not been sent to it yet.
suggested_refs: The unlocated studio of Nicolas Stéphane Sonrel, military physician and amateur painter, at Tours

stops.name: Tours, L'Hiver
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the fr.wiki gallery list; month and day unknown
stops.campa: At sixteen she paints Winter, the earliest canvas the record keeps under her name. It comes before Paris and before Lefebvre, and it carries a year and nothing else: no month recorded, no exhibition, no buyer. A girl in a provincial town paints the coldest of the four seasons and puts it away, and a century later the lists of her work still open on it. The veiled women and the slow processions she will be known for are all still ahead of her, and so is every jury that will judge them.
suggested_refs: L'Hiver, 1890, earliest dated work in the fr.wiki gallery list

stops.name: Musée des Beaux-Arts de Tours, Pax et Labor
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown
stops.campa: Her terminal exam piece is titled Peace and Labour, and it comes home to Tours to hang in the old episcopal palace beside the cathedral. Two words for a working life, and she keeps both: sixty years of steady production, and no scandal attached to her name in any of it. The museum still holds the canvas. It is the first institutional trace of a career that will run past 1940, and the last thing Tours can claim of her before Paris, and then Sceaux, take her for good.
suggested_refs: Pax et Labor, 1892, Musée des Beaux-Arts de Tours, 18 place François-Sicard

segments.name: The Académie Julian and the First Salons

stops.name: Passage des Panoramas, the atelier of Jules Lefebvre
stops.date_confidence: contested: fr.wiki names the Académie Julian with no year at all; the 1891-1892 span comes from Wikidata, which attaches it to the École des Beaux-Arts, an institution that admitted no women until 1897. Wikidata also names Gustave Boulanger as her teacher, who died in 1888
stops.campa: She goes to Paris to finish her training at the Académie Julian, in the atelier of Jules Lefebvre. The Julian takes women seriously enough to criticise their work as it criticises anyone's, which the École des Beaux-Arts will not do for another six years. Below the studios the glass-roofed arcade goes on selling engravings and gloves, indifferent to what is drawn overhead. She is not yet twenty, and she is learning an academic line she will spend the rest of her life bending toward something older.
stops.quote: Elle part a Paris parfaire sa formation artistique a l'Academie Julian dans l'atelier de Jules Lefebvre.
suggested_refs: Enrolment registers of the Académie Julian, ateliers for women, early 1890s
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Élisabeth Sonrel' (names the École des Beaux-Arts instead)
French Wikipedia, 'École nationale supérieure des beaux-arts' (women admitted from 1897)

stops.name: Palais de l'Industrie, the Salon debut
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Clement (1904); the month is the Salon's ordinary May opening
stops.campa: At eighteen she hangs at the Salon des Artistes Français for the first time, and the jury gives her an honorable mention. The Palais de l'Industrie is the machine of official French art, thousands of canvases stacked to the cornice, and a mention here means a name has been picked out of that wall. Her father's pupil is a Paris exhibitor now. She will keep coming back to this Salon for forty-eight years, through a war that closes it altogether and an occupation that does not.
suggested_refs: Salon des Artistes Français, livret of 1893, Palais de l'Industrie, Champs-Élysées
sources: Clara Erskine Clement, Women in the Fine Arts (1904), entry 'Sonrel, Mlle. E.'

stops.name: Paris, the working painter
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, and no address is named in any reachable source
stops.campa: From this year she is no longer a student from Tours visiting the capital; she lives and sells in Paris. The street she keeps in these first years is not named in anything that survives. What is recorded is the choice of materials: watercolour and gouache rather than oil, thin and luminous, the medium of illustrators and of missals, and the one that will carry nearly everything she is remembered for. It is an unfashionable decision in a city that measures seriousness in oil.
suggested_refs: Paris trade and artist directories of the 1890s, for Sonrel's first professional address

stops.name: Palais de l'Industrie, Âmes errantes
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown
stops.campa: Wandering Souls goes up at the Salon, and with it the register she is making her own: allegory, drift, the female figure carrying something larger than a likeness. In the same year she paints a Virgin and Child. The mystical subject and the devotional one will run side by side in her work for the next forty years without ever quite merging. How the jury or the press received either canvas is recorded nowhere reachable. Only that they hung, in that year, in that building.
suggested_refs: Âmes errantes, Salon of 1894; Vierge à l'enfant, 1894

stops.name: Palais de l'Industrie, the third-class medal
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Clement (1904); month and day unknown
stops.campa: Two years after the honorable mention the Salon gives her a third-class medal, the first metal of her career. An American compiler, Clara Erskine Clement, will set the three awards down in a single line in 1904: mention in 1893, third-class medal in 1895, bronze at the Paris Exposition in 1900. Her list stops there. Whatever the next forty-six years of exhibiting bring, they bring no distinction that the standard survey of women painters thought worth printing.
stops.quote: SONREL, MLLE. E. Honorable mention, Paris, 1893; third-class medal, 1895; bronze medal, Paris Exposition, 1900.
stops.quote_source: Clara Erskine Clement, Women in the Fine Arts (1904)
suggested_refs: Clement's Women in the Fine Arts (1904), the only period compilation of her awards reached
sources: Clara Erskine Clement, Women in the Fine Arts (1904)

stops.name: Sceaux, the studio that holds for life
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown
stops.campa: She sets up her own studio at Sceaux, south of Paris, in a town whose park was laid out for Colbert. Paris is close enough for the Salons and far enough for the work. The address holds for fifty-eight years: she paints here, receives here, grows old here, and dies here. Everything after this is a departure and a return: to Italy once, to Brittany many times over thirty years, to the Champs-Élysées every spring. She never afterward needs another address.
suggested_refs: Sceaux, Hauts-de-Seine, and the parc de Sceaux laid out for Colbert

stops.name: Florence, in front of the Quattrocento
stops.date_confidence: undated in every reachable source; both encyclopedias place the Italian journey loosely in the 1890s, and this year is a placeholder inside that decade
stops.campa: She stands in front of Botticelli long enough that the rest of her life is spent being compared to him. The processions of pale women, the linear grace, the flowers held like sentences: critics date all of it to this city rather than to any Paris atelier. The English painters who went the same way a generation earlier, Dante Gabriel Rossetti and Edward Burne-Jones, give those critics their phrase for her, the Pre-Raphaelite of French Symbolism. No document ties her to Rossetti or Burne-Jones. The comparison is made over her head, by critics who recognise the same Florentine source in all three.
suggested_refs: The Uffizi Botticellis, cited in both encyclopedias as the source of her mature manner

stops.name: Rome, the second half of the Italian journey
stops.date_confidence: undated; paired with Florence in every account and fixed to no year by any of them
stops.campa: Rome is the second half of the Italian journey, named in every account of her formation and itemised in none. What she looked at there, which collections, which frescoes, which weeks, no source says; the sources give a destination and an effect and nothing in between. She comes back to France with the academic realism of the Julian loosened in her hand and something older set in its place, and begins painting virgins who look as though they were drawn four hundred years before she was born.
suggested_refs: The Roman leg of the Italian journey, unspecified in the sources as to collections or dates

stops.name: Sceaux, Le Sommeil de la Vierge
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, and no source places the painting of it at Sceaux rather than in Paris
stops.campa: The Sleep of the Virgin is painted in the year she takes the Sceaux studio, and it waits five years for its reward. The canvas exists first and quietly; the machinery of Salons and expositions catches up with it five years later, or, for most of her work, never. The subject is a sleeping woman and a mystery, handled without drama, the way she handles everything. In 1900 it takes a bronze medal at the Exposition Universelle, and it is the only canvas of hers that any jury is recorded as naming.
suggested_refs: Le Sommeil de la Vierge, 1895, crowned at the Exposition Universelle of 1900

stops.name: Sceaux, Les Rameaux
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the fr.wiki gallery caption; no source states where it was painted or that it hung at the Salon, and the Ashmolean record that claims a Salon showing places that Salon in a building not yet built
stops.campa: Palm Sunday, watercolour on laid paper, nearly a metre wide: a procession of young women in the pale processional manner that is now unmistakably hers. The gallery lists give the year and nothing else, no jury, no room, no notice. A hundred and twenty-three years later the Ashmolean Museum at Oxford will take the sheet into its collection, and the institution holding her best-known surviving watercolour will be one she never saw, in the country whose painters gave the critics their name for her.
suggested_refs: Les Rameaux, 1897, watercolour on laid paper, 52.7 x 90.8 cm, Ashmolean Museum WA2020.16

stops.name: Saint-Étienne, the looms of the Maison Neyret
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown
stops.campa: The ribbon and picture weavers of Saint-Étienne put her Flore on the loom, black and white on a white ground, and her allegorical women come off the canvas as woven silk. Four such pieces end in the town's Musée d'Art et d'Industrie. Whether she travels down to watch the looms or posts the design and waits, nothing says. What the commission proves is that by the end of the century her images circulate as objects, on silk, on postcards, in almanacs, far past the reach of any Salon wall.
stops.quote: des images en soie tissees sont realisees par la Maison Neyret (quatre pieces a Saint-Etienne, Musee d'Art et d'Industrie, notamment Flore, noir et blanc sur fond blanc, 1899)
suggested_refs: The four Sonrel silk pictures at the Musée d'Art et d'Industrie, Saint-Étienne

stops.name: Paris, Les Esprits de l'abîme at the Salon
stops.date_confidence: year and Salon showing attested; the venue is unknown, so the pin is the Paris centroid and not a building
stops.campa: The Spirits of the Abyss is the darkest title in her known catalogue, proof that the mysticism is not only bridal veils and spring gardens. Where it hung is a real hole in the record: the Palais de l'Industrie came down two years earlier to clear ground for the coming world's fair, and the Grand Palais that replaces it will not house this Salon until 1901. The canvas is certain, the year is certain, the room is lost. Seventy-five years on, this same watercolour will bring her back from oblivion.
suggested_refs: Livrets of the Salons of 1898 to 1900, held at the Champ-de-Mars during the rebuilding of the Champs-Élysées site
sources: French Wikipedia, 'Palais de l'Industrie' (Salon use 1857-1897, demolition 1896-97)

stops.name: Grand Palais, the Exposition Universelle
stops.date_confidence: year attested and corroborated by Clement (1904); month and day unknown
stops.campa: At the world's fair the five-year-old Sleep of the Virgin takes a bronze medal, and in the same season the Académie des Beaux-Arts gives her the Henri Lehmann prize, three thousand francs. The two honours are separate: one belongs to the Exposition and to that canvas, the other to the Académie, and no source joins them. Millions cross Paris that year for the machinery halls and the colonial pavilions. A provincial doctor's daughter is medalled among them, and Clement's list of her distinctions ends here.
stops.quote: Lors de l'Exposition universelle de 1900, elle obtient une medaille de bronze pour sa toile Le Sommeil de la Vierge, ainsi que le prix Henri Lehmann de 3000 francs par l'Academie des beaux-arts.
suggested_refs: Award lists of the Exposition Universelle of 1900; the Henri Lehmann prize of the Académie des Beaux-Arts
sources: Clara Erskine Clement, Women in the Fine Arts (1904)

stops.name: Sceaux, Jeune femme au chaperon
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the work's own inscription; no exhibition record and no place of making are known, so the pin is her studio by default
stops.campa: A young woman in a headdress, painted in the year she turns thirty. The date is firm and everything around it is missing: no Salon record, no buyer, no room. That is the ordinary condition of her catalogue, works dated by their own inscriptions and floating free of any exhibition history. She is eleven years into her Salon career and has settled into the visual language she will not leave: the veiled head, the flowers, the stillness borrowed from fresco painting.
suggested_refs: Young Woman with a Headdress, 1904, dated by inscription and unattached to any Salon

stops.name: London, Women Painters of the World
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the place of publication is not stated in the source, so this pin is an inference
stops.campa: A survey volume gathers the women painters of the world between two covers, and she is in it. The book fixes her, at thirty-one, as an established name inside a category that will later be dissolved and forgotten: not a French painter but a woman painter, entered in a register kept separately from the main one. The rediscovery of 1974 will have to start from exactly this kind of shelf. Where the volume was printed the source does not say, and the placing here is a guess.
suggested_refs: Women Painters of the World (1905), the survey volume naming Sonrel

stops.name: Paimpont, the forest of Brocéliande
stops.date_confidence: circa; the sources say the Breton travels begin around 1900 without naming a month or a first visit
stops.campa: From about this year she goes to Brittany regularly, and the forest of Paimpont, which the romances call Brocéliande, becomes one of her recurring grounds. Merlin's wood, Arthurian country, the one French forest with a reputation to match the subjects she has been painting in a Paris studio for a decade. The medieval matter she took from books and from Italian panels she can now walk into. She returns for the next thirty years, and the Breton work never stops.
suggested_refs: The forest of Paimpont, identified with the Brocéliande of the Arthurian romances

stops.name: Concarneau, the Ville Close
stops.date_confidence: circa; fr.wiki groups Concarneau with the earliest Breton destinations without a year
stops.campa: The walled town sits on its island in the harbour, ringed by ramparts, with the sardine fleet working around it. Concarneau is one of the first Breton places she paints and one of the last: she comes back to it across thirty years. In this first wave the coast serves mostly as a setting, somewhere to stand her allegorical figures where the light is better. What the town is actually doing, the boats, the drying nets, the women on the quay, waits another decade for her attention.
suggested_refs: The Ville Close of Concarneau and its sardine port, painted in both of her Breton phases

stops.name: Pont-l'Abbé, the lacemaker of the Bigouden country
stops.date_confidence: circa; the town is attested in the first Breton group, but the lacemaker watercolour itself carries no date, so its phase cannot be settled
stops.campa: Capital of the Bigouden country, where the women wear the tallest coiffe in Brittany and the lace workshops keep half the town employed. She paints a young lacemaker of Pont-l'Abbé, turning the region's own craft into her subject, and the Bigouden headdress enters her vocabulary alongside the veils of her virgins. The sitters here have an occupation as well as a costume, and for the first time in her work the woman in the picture is doing something with her hands.
suggested_refs: Jeune dentellière de Pont-l'Abbé, undated, in the fr.wiki gallery list

stops.name: Loctudy, a name on a list of four
stops.date_confidence: circa; attested only as one of the early Breton destinations, with no year and no work attached
stops.campa: A fishing port at the mouth of the Pont-l'Abbé river, named in the record as one of the earliest Breton destinations and then left bare. What she painted at Loctudy is not itemised; the canvases from this coast are catalogued as costume studies and marines with their harbours detached. The town is a name on a list of four, and the list is the whole of the evidence. She is working her way along the southern Finistère shore, town by town, in the years when the Salon still expects allegory from her.
suggested_refs: Loctudy, named by fr.wiki among the first Breton destinations and by nothing else

stops.name: Plougastel-Daoulas, the coiffes of the peninsula
stops.date_confidence: circa; fr.wiki names Plougastel in both the early group and the post-1910 list, so the first visit is undated
stops.campa: A peninsula parish shut off by the Elorn and the roadstead of Brest, known for its strawberry fields and its stone calvary, and known to painters because the isolation has kept the costume intact. She paints the young women in coiffe and apron with the same careful line she gives allegorical virgins in Paris. Plougastel is the northern end of her Breton range; from here the road back to Sceaux is a long day, and the light is nothing at all like the Loire's.
suggested_refs: The calvary and costume of Plougastel-Daoulas, Finistère

stops.name: Cap Sizun, the girl on the peninsula
stops.date_confidence: the watercolour carries no date at all; the year here is a placeholder inside her Breton decades, and the Pointe du Van pin is inferred from the toponym, not from any source
stops.campa: A watercolour titled Young Girl of the Cap Sizun puts her somewhere on this granite peninsula, wind-scoured, running west between two headlands to the open Atlantic. The work names the region and nothing narrower, and it carries no year; the Pointe du Van at its western tip is the likeliest ground and stays a guess. What is left of the work is a girl, a peninsula and a single sheet of paper, with no owner, no exhibition and no second version recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: Jeune fille du Cap Sizun, watercolour on paper, undated, fr.wiki gallery list

stops.name: Concarneau, the brighter palette
stops.date_confidence: the sources date the shift to 1910 as a starting point, not to a single visit
stops.campa: From this year the Breton work changes register. The allegories thin out and the daily life comes forward: portraits, quays, sunlight, a palette that has stopped being pale. Concarneau, familiar for a decade already, is named again among the towns she returns to under the new manner. The sardine port that had been a backdrop becomes something nearer the subject. She is thirty-six, twenty years into exhibiting, and she is changing how she paints without changing where she goes.
stops.quote: a partir de 1910, elle realise egalement des vues des villes cotieres de Plougastel-Daoulas, Pont-l'Abbe, Le Faouet et Concarneau.
suggested_refs: The post-1910 Breton views: Plougastel-Daoulas, Pont-l'Abbé, Le Faouët, Concarneau

stops.name: Plougastel-Daoulas, the peninsula painted twice
stops.date_confidence: attested as part of the post-1910 group; no individual visit is dated
stops.campa: She comes back to the peninsula with a warmer hand. The same calvary, the same coiffes, the same women, rendered now in vivid colour and direct observation rather than as costume standing in for allegory. The record puts Plougastel-Daoulas in both waves of her Breton travel, which makes it the clearest measure of what twenty years did to her eye: one place painted twice, by a Symbolist first and by something much nearer a naturalist afterward. The calvary stands where it stood. She has learned to look at it without needing it to mean anything else.
suggested_refs: Plougastel-Daoulas, named in both the early and the post-1910 Breton lists

stops.name: Pont-l'Abbé, the second passage
stops.date_confidence: attested as part of the post-1910 group; no individual visit is dated
stops.campa: Pont-l'Abbé is named again in the later list of Breton towns she paints, with Plougastel-Daoulas, Le Faouët and Concarneau. She is a familiar figure on this coast by now rather than a visitor down from the capital, working the same market squares and lace workshops she first saw around 1900. The Bigouden coiffe that was an exotic silhouette in her early Breton sheets has become, in the later ones, simply what the women in her pictures wear. Nothing in the record says where she lodges on these journeys, or with whom.
suggested_refs: Pont-l'Abbé in the post-1910 list of Breton town views

stops.name: Le Faouët, the collection that stays
stops.date_confidence: attested as part of the post-1910 group; the museum's acquisitions are not individually dated in any reachable source
stops.campa: Inland in the Morbihan, known for its pardons and its vast timber market hall, Le Faouët is the odd name in a list the record calls coastal: it has no coast. She goes back often enough that the local museum ends by holding a lasting collection of her work, and those holdings are now the best evidence of how much time she actually spent painting in Brittany rather than passing through it. Salon livrets can build a Paris reputation on paper. The Faouët holdings are the pictures themselves, still in the town where she painted them.
suggested_refs: The Sonrel holdings of the musée du Faouët, Morbihan

stops.name: Sceaux, the Virgin between Geneviève and Joan of Arc
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month, day and place of making unknown
stops.campa: In the third year of the war she paints a Virgin and Child between Saint Geneviève and Joan of Arc: the patroness who turned the Huns from Paris, and the girl who lifted the siege of Orléans, standing on either side of the Mother of God. The Salon is shut for the duration and there is nowhere to hang it. She paints the two military saints of France anyway, at Sceaux, eleven kilometres south of a capital in its third year of war, in the manner she learned in Florence.
suggested_refs: Virgin and Child, Between Saint Geneviève and Joan of Arc, 1916
sources: French Wikipedia, 'Salon des artistes français' (Salon interrupted for the First World War)

stops.name: Sceaux, Notre-Dame du Cerfeuil
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the work's own record; no exhibition and no place of making are known
stops.campa: Our Lady of the Cow Parsley: a wayside Madonna wreathed in the commonest hedgerow plant in France, watercolour with bodycolour over pencil, forty-five centimetres by thirty-eight. The title folds a weed into a Marian devotion, the same operation she has been running on hedgerows and garden flowers since the 1890s. She is forty-nine. No exhibition record attaches to the sheet, and it passes into a private collection, which is where most of her late work goes and stays.
suggested_refs: Notre-Dame du Cerfeuil, 1923, watercolour with bodycolour over pencil, 45 x 38 cm, private collection
sources: Wikimedia Commons record for the 1923 watercolour

stops.name: La Baule-Escoublac, the villa by the sea
stops.date_confidence: decade only: both encyclopedias say the 1930s and no source fixes a year, so 1930 here stands for the decade
stops.campa: She has a villa built at La Baule, on the Atlantic edge of the Breton country she has been painting for thirty years. It is the only address she keeps outside Sceaux and Paris, and the first time in six decades of work that she builds a house instead of taking rooms for a painting season. The resort is fashionable, the pines run down to a long beach, and the record fixes the decade and refuses the year. She is in her late fifties, and no source records her going anywhere new after this.
stops.quote: Dans les annees 1930, elle se fait construire une villa a La Baule.
stops.quote_source: French Wikipedia, 'Élisabeth Sonrel' (accents normalised), sourced there to bretagne.com
suggested_refs: The Sonrel villa at La Baule-Escoublac, built in the 1930s

stops.name: Turnhout, the Missel de Lourdes
stops.date_confidence: year and town attested; the publishing house is not named in the source, and the attribution to Brepols is an inference from the city
stops.campa: The Missal of Lourdes, dedicated to the faithful servants of Mary, is printed at Turnhout in the Belgian Campine, a town whose presses have supplied liturgical books to half of Catholic Europe. Her illustrations go into it and out through it into devotional hands well beyond France. Nothing suggests she travels there; the connection is the printed object, sent and returned by post. She is fifty-eight, and her images have been circulating as reproductions for thirty years.
stops.quote: Missel de Lourdes, dedie aux fideles serviteurs de Marie, Turnhout, (1932)
stops.quote_source: French Wikipedia, 'Élisabeth Sonrel', bibliography of illustrated works (accents normalised)
suggested_refs: Missel de Lourdes, Turnhout, 1932; and the earlier Missel des Saintes Femmes de France, Tours, c. 1900

stops.name: Sceaux, Vase d'anémones
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month, day and place of making unknown
stops.campa: A vase of anemones, painted in her sixty-seventh year, in an occupied country. No virgins, no processions, no Breton coiffes: flowers in a vase, and a studio window with an occupied city on the other side of it. It is the last dated work the record keeps of her, and she has twelve more years to live. Whatever she makes after this, in the Sceaux studio she took in 1895, nobody has counted and no catalogue lists. Fifty-one years of dated work end in a gap where a last decade should be.
suggested_refs: Vase d'anémones, 1941, last dated work in the fr.wiki gallery list

stops.name: Grand Palais, the last Salon
stops.date_confidence: year attested as her last recorded Salon; month and day unknown
stops.campa: She hangs at the Salon des Artistes Français for the last recorded time, in the second year of the German occupation of Paris. Forty-eight years separate this showing from the honorable mention of 1893, but the span is not a run: the Salon shut for the First World War. No press notice, no farewell, no listed title survives from the final appearance. The record gives the year and stops. Forty-eight years of exhibiting end with an entry in a livret and nothing else.
stops.quote: sauf pendant la premiere guerre mondiale ou le Salon a ete interrompu
stops.quote_source: French Wikipedia, 'Salon des artistes français' (accents normalised)
suggested_refs: Salon des Artistes Français, livret of 1941, occupied Paris

stops.name: Sceaux, death in the studio town
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: She dies at Sceaux at seventy-eight, in the town where she opened her studio fifty-eight years before. She had been a Salon exhibitor while the Palais de l'Industrie was still standing, and she lived to see the Fourth Republic. The obscurity begins almost at once. Within a few years the name that carried a bronze medal from the Exposition Universelle, and a place in a world survey of women painters, is one the dealers no longer recognise when it comes across a table.
suggested_refs: Death record of Sceaux, Hauts-de-Seine, 9 February 1953

stops.name: Cimetière de Sceaux, the grave on the rue Houdan
stops.date_confidence: the burial is attested but its date is not recorded; it is dated here to her death
stops.campa: She is buried in the cemetery at 174 rue Houdan, in the town where she took a studio in 1895 and worked for the fifty-eight years after. The date of the burial is recorded nowhere reachable; only the death, on 9 February 1953, is fixed. Her whole working geography fits into four names: Tours, Paris, Brittany, Sceaux. What the stone says, and whether it still stands, no source reports, and the queries that would answer it come back blocked. The cemetery keeps its own list of notable dead, and she is not on it.

stops.name: Hôtel Drouot, the sale that returns her
stops.date_confidence: date attested in the fr.wiki footnote, which is itself unsourced
stops.campa: Twenty-one years after her death The Spirits of the Abyss comes up at the Hôtel Drouot and sells for a price that startles the room. The auction is credited with the rediscovery: from this sale the dealers come back, then the collectors, then the catalogues. The watercolour that does it is the darkest thing she ever painted, shown at a Salon in 1899 whose very room has since been lost from the record. French Wikipedia notes the recovery in a footnote it does not source.
stops.quote: Malgre son succes toute sa vie, la peintre est rapidement oubliee et redecouverte seulement a partir de 1974.

stops.campa: A local historical bulletin prints a study called Élisabeth Sonrel, 1874 to 1953, a forgotten Symbolist artist. The town that housed her for fifty-eight years is the one that takes her back first, ahead of the museums and well ahead of the reference works. The study itself is not reachable outside the bulletin's own pages. A neighbourhood historical society, not a museum and not a national catalogue, is what puts her name back into print under the word Symbolist.

stops.name: Ashmolean Museum, Oxford: Les Rameaux accessioned
stops.date_confidence: inferred from the accession number WA2020.16; no acquisition date is stated in the museum record
stops.campa: Palm Sunday, painted in 1897, enters the Ashmolean Museum at Oxford: a French Symbolist watercolour in an English collection, in the country whose Pre-Raphaelites gave the critics their phrase for her. It is the clearest institutional holding of her work outside France, and it arrives a hundred and twenty-three years after the sheet was made and sixty-seven after her death. Her name is back in a catalogue, spelled correctly, with an accession number against it.
